claim.pdf_says: Page 566 (printed 536) OPENS with the continuation of 14.5.3.3 item 1): 'b)   the next-encountered statement-name, or' then 'c)   a separator period.' - each printed as its own indented sub-item, before item '2) for a single imperative statement contained within another statement, by'.
claim.markdown_says: Those two sub-items appear BEFORE the '' anchor, appended to sub-item a) as one run-on line at the end of the page-565 slice: " a) any element that follows the exhaustion of the statement's syntax, or b) the next-encountered statement-name, or c) a separator period." The page-566 slice then starts at '2) for a single imperative statement contained within another statement, by'.
claim.why_it_matters: Two effects. (1) Page attribution: text printed on page 536/566 is filed under the page-565 anchor, so a citation of the form 'p.536 item 1) c)' resolves to the wrong page anchor. (2) List structure: the three-way choice a)/b)/c) of 14.5.3.3 rule 1) is flattened into a single paragraph, whereas the parallel rules 2) and 4) on the same page keep a)/b)/c) as separate items. 14.5.3.3 is the normative rule for implicit scope termination, which the parser's statement-scope resolution is built from.

verdict.reasoning: Both source descriptions are factually accurate, but the difference is confined to page-boundary slicing and list line-breaking - it is page-break furniture, not a content discrepancy. WHAT I INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED. Rendered PDF p.566 (printed 536) at 300dpi: the page does open with two indented sub-items, and reading the printed glyphs directly I see 'b)' followed by 'the next-encountered statement-name, or', then 'c)' followed by 'a separator period.', at the same sub-item indent used by 2)a-c and 4)a-b lower on the same page. Rendered PDF p.565 (printed 535): its last text line is 'a) any element that follows the exhaustion of the statement's syntax, or', so the page break falls exactly between sub-item a) and sub-item b). Markdown (specs/ISO_COBOL.md, verified with cat -A): line 23660 reads ' a) any element that follows the exhaustion of the statement's syntax, or b) the next-encountered statement-name, or c) a separator period.' and the '' anchor follows at line 23662. So the claim misquotes neither source. WHY IT IS STILL NOT A REAL FINDING. (1) Nothing is missing. Every word, both choice indicators 'b)' and 'c)', and both 'or' connectives survive verbatim in the markdown, in correct reading order. This is precisely the reject case 'the missing text is actually present, reflowed onto an adjacent line'. No choice indicator was lost - I looked at the printed glyphs and both 'b)' and 'c)' appear intact on the markdown line. (2) Meaning is unchanged. 'by a) X, or b) Y, or c) Z.' expresses the identical three-way disjunction as the three separate list items; a reader deriving implicit-scope-termination rules for the parser gets exactly the same rule either way. There is no ambiguity introduced, because the a)/b)/c) labels and the 'or' connectives are all still there marking the alternation. (3) The two residual differences - which side of the page-566 anchor two lines sit on, and whether a)/b)/c) are separate lines or one - are exactly the enumerated reject categories 'page-break furniture' and 'formatting / line wrapping'. This is the textbook artifact of a PDF-to-markdown extractor joining list continuation lines across a page boundary. (4) The claimed citation harm is overstated. The section anchor 'section-14-5-3-3' correctly precedes the whole of rule 1), and this project's doctrine cites by section/GR ('14.5.3.3 rule 1)c)'), not by page anchor; the page anchors are navigational. (5) I also diffed the remainder of the page-566 slice against the render - items 2)a-c, 3), 4)a-b, the 'Any phrase encountered' paragraph, 'A contained statement is also referred to as a nested statement.', 14.6, 14.6.1 and its four paragraphs all match, including the comma-not-'or' ending of 2)a). No other discrepancy exists on this page. Verdict: cosmetic page-break artifact, not a structural content discrepancy; severity 'structural' is not warranted.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. The observation itself is accurate - PDF p.566 (printed 536) opens with sub-items 'b) the next-encountered statement-name, or' and 'c) a separator period.', and the markdown carries both on the preceding line, ahead of the page-566 anchor - but this is a page-boundary line-join artifact, the class of difference explicitly excluded as page-break furniture / formatting. All text, both choice indicators b) and c), and both 'or' connectives are present in correct reading order, and the normative content of 14.5.3.3 rule 1) is fully and unambiguously preserved. If anyone wants the transcription cosmetically tidied for list-style consistency with sibling rules 2) and 4), that is a low-value formatting cleanup (split the run-on line into three items and move b) and c) after the page-566 anchor), not a spec-fidelity defect, and it has no effect on any semantics the parser's statement-scope resolution is derived from.
